# sysutils_hosts_entry (Resource)

Manages one line of `/etc/hosts` that maps an IP address to hostnames. All other lines, comments and blank lines are kept, and so are the file's mode, owner and group. Changes are written atomically. On destroy, only the managed line is removed.

Each resource owns one line. Several resources can manage different lines of the same file, and lines added by hand, by the distribution or by other tools stay as they are. Unlike [`sysutils_file_line`](./file_line.md), it understands the file format: it validates addresses and hostnames, finds its line however it is spaced, and refuses to map a name that another line already resolves.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Map a private address to a fully qualified name and a short alias.
resource "sysutils_hosts_entry" "db" {
  ip        = "10.0.0.5"
  hostnames = ["db.internal.example.com", "db"]
  comment   = "primary database"
}

# IPv6 works the same way.
resource "sysutils_hosts_entry" "db_v6" {
  ip        = "fd00::5"
  hostnames = ["db.internal.example.com", "db"]
}

# Point a name at loopback. The distribution's "127.0.0.1 localhost" line
# has another canonical name and is left alone.
resource "sysutils_hosts_entry" "app_local" {
  ip        = "127.0.0.1"
  hostnames = ["app.local"]
}

# A hosts file other than /etc/hosts, such as one served by dnsmasq's
# addn-hosts option.
resource "sysutils_hosts_entry" "printer" {
  path      = "/etc/dnsmasq.hosts"
  ip        = "192.168.1.20"
  hostnames = ["printer.lan", "printer"]
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `hostnames` (List of String) Hostnames for `ip`, in order. The first is the canonical name, which reverse lookups of `ip` return; the others are aliases. Each must be a hostname as defined by RFC 1123: labels of letters, digits and hyphens separated by dots, without a trailing dot. Names must be unique, ignoring case. The line whose address is `ip` and whose first hostname is the first of these, ignoring case, is the managed line.
- `ip` (String) IPv4 address in dotted-decimal form, such as `"10.0.0.5"`, or IPv6 address, such as `"fd00::5"`, without a zone. Compared as an address, so `"fd00::5"` also finds a line written as `fd00:0:0:0:0:0:0:5`. Changing it rewrites the managed line in place.

### Optional

- `allow_duplicate` (Boolean) Allow a hostname that another line already maps to a different address of the same family (IPv4 or IPv6). By default applying fails in that case, because the resolver returns the first matching line and the managed line might never be used. Defaults to `false`.
- `comment` (String) Comment written at the end of the line after `#`, such as `"managed by Terraform"`. Must be a non-empty single line without leading or trailing white space. Unset means no comment.
- `path` (String) Absolute path of the hosts file, inside the provider's `root_dir` if set. Created with mode `0644` if it does not exist; its directory must exist. A symlink at `path` is refused. Defaults to `"/etc/hosts"`. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) `<path>:<ip>`.

## File Format

The file is read as described in `hosts(5)`. A `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A line is an entry if what is left holds an IP address followed by at least one hostname, separated by spaces or tabs. Blank lines, comment lines, commented-out entries and lines without a valid address or without a hostname are not entries; they, and every entry the resource does not manage, are kept byte for byte.

## The Managed Line

The managed line is the entry whose address is `ip` and whose first hostname (the canonical name) is the first of `hostnames`, ignoring case. The address is compared as an address, so `fd00::5` also finds `fd00:0:0:0:0:0:0:5`.

Matching on the canonical name as well as the address lets several entries share an address: a resource for `127.0.0.1` with `hostnames = ["app.local"]` adds its own line and leaves the distribution's `127.0.0.1 localhost` alone. To manage names on an existing line, import it, or list its canonical name first.

- **Create** appends the line to the end of the file. If a line with the same address and canonical name exists already, it is taken over and rewritten in place instead.
- **Update** rewrites the line in place, even if `ip` or the first hostname changes. It keeps the line's indentation, the white space after the address and between names, the spelling of an unchanged address (such as upper-case IPv6 digits) and of an unchanged comment. A new line uses the white space after the address of the file's first entry, or a tab if there is none; names are separated by a space and the comment by ` # `.
- Further lines with the same address and canonical name, such as a copy added by hand, are removed whenever the line is written, so that a stale copy can't shadow it.
- **Destroy** removes the line (and any such copy), and leaves the rest of the file in place, even if it ends up empty.

## Duplicate Hostnames

The resolver returns the first line that maps a name. If another line already maps one of `hostnames` to a different address, the managed line might never be used, so apply fails and names the conflicting line, without changing the file. Set `allow_duplicate = true` to add the entry anyway.

Names are compared ignoring case. Only addresses of the same family conflict: a name with one IPv4 and one IPv6 address, such as `localhost` with `127.0.0.1` and `::1`, is the normal dual-stack setup. Lines with the managed address itself never conflict. The check runs on create and update, not on refresh: a conflicting line added later shows up the next time the entry is written.

## Writing the File

- Nothing is written if the file already holds the entry, so the modification time only changes when content does. Changes in spacing alone are not drift and are not undone.
- Line endings are kept: in a file with CRLF line endings (judged by its first line), the new line ends with CRLF too. A file without a line break at the end gets one when a line is appended.
- Changes are written atomically, exactly as by [`sysutils_file_line`](./file_line.md#writing-the-file): the replacement gets the original file's owner, group, mode, ACLs and SELinux label before it is renamed into place, and the edit fails without writing if the file was changed by someone else in the meantime. Several resources editing the same file, including `sysutils_file_line` and `sysutils_ini_value`, are serialised by the provider, so they can be applied in parallel safely.
- A missing file is created with mode `0644`, owned by the user running Terraform. Its directory must exist.
- With the provider's [`root_dir`](../index.md#root-directory) set, `path` is inside the root: `/etc/hosts` means `<root_dir>/etc/hosts`, which is how an image's hosts file is prepared. `path` and `id` keep the path inside the root.
- Files larger than 64 MiB are refused.

## Drift Detection

On refresh, the provider reads the file and looks up the managed line:

- If its hostnames or comment were changed outside Terraform, the actual ones are recorded, and the plan shows an in-place update back to the configuration. Hostnames are compared exactly, including case and order.
- If the line was removed, or its address or canonical name changed so that it is no longer the managed line, or the file was deleted, the resource is removed from state and the plan shows it being created again.

## Import

An existing line can be imported with the path of the file and the address, separated by a colon. The path ends at the first colon, so IPv6 addresses need no quoting, but paths containing colons cannot be imported:

```shell
# <path>:<ip>; the first line of the file that maps the address is imported.
terraform import sysutils_hosts_entry.db '/etc/hosts:10.0.0.5'

# The path ends at the first colon, so an IPv6 address needs no quoting.
terraform import sysutils_hosts_entry.db_v6 '/etc/hosts:fd00::5'
```

If several lines map the address, the first one is imported, with a warning. To pick another one, add its canonical name after a comma, such as `/etc/hosts:127.0.0.1,app.local`.

## Caveats

- Consistent with the provider's [security model](../index.md#security-model), a symlink at `path` is refused, and so is anything else that is not a regular file. Symlinks in the parent components of `path` are followed (inside the root if `root_dir` is set). On destroy, a symlink or other non-regular file at `path` is left untouched, with a warning.
- The rename gives the file a new inode, which breaks hard links. If `path` is a mount point, as `/etc/hosts` is in Docker containers, the file is rewritten in place, which is not atomic. See [`sysutils_file_line`](./file_line.md#caveats) for details.
- Preserving an owner other than the user running Terraform requires the privileges to `chown` the replacement file, normally root.
- Addresses with a zone, such as `fe80::1%eth0`, and hostnames that are not valid under RFC 1123 (with underscores, a trailing dot or non-ASCII letters) are refused. Such lines already in the file are kept but can't be managed.
- Two resources with the same address and canonical name, or a `sysutils_file` managing the same file, conflict with each other.
- The resource only works on Unix-like systems.
